documents.abstract: The rapid development of artificial intelligence has significantly transformed higher education and foreign language learning. In particular, the increasing use of generative artificial intelligence applications such as ChatGPT, Grammarly, Google Gemini, and other AI-powered educational platforms has created new opportunities for university students studying English as a Foreign Language (EFL). These technologies provide support for academic writing, vocabulary development, grammar correction, translation, reading comprehension, and independent learning. However, effective engagement with artificial intelligence requires more than the ability to operate digital applications. Students also need AI literacy, which involves understanding how AI systems function, evaluating AI-generated information, recognizing technological limitations, and using these tools responsibly and ethically. The present study examines AI literacy among university EFL students, focusing on their perceptions, everyday practices, and challenges associated with AI-assisted language learning. A qualitative literature-based research design is employed to synthesize relevant theoretical frameworks and empirical findings concerning AI literacy in higher education and foreign language education. Particular attention is given to students' familiarity with AI applications, purposes of use, critical evaluation skills, ethical awareness, and digital learning competencies. Recent empirical research by Hossain, Çelik, and Hiniz (2025), involving 427 Turkish university EFL students, revealed moderate AI familiarity and considerable reliance on AI tools for translation and grammatical proofreading. The findings also highlighted limited understanding of AI mechanisms and concerns regarding plagiarism and academic integrity. Similarly, UNESCO's AI Competency Framework for Students emphasizes the importance of human-centered thinking, ethical awareness, and responsible interaction with AI technologies. The study argues that AI literacy should become an essential component of contemporary EFL education. It concludes that universities should provide systematic AI literacy instruction to help students move from simple technological use toward critical, informed, and responsible engagement with artificial intelligence.

As generative artificial intelligence becomes one of the most significant systems of knowledge production in our society today, questions relating to who can access and shape that production grow increasingly important in our discourse. This paper argues that the existing frameworks for AI literacy, which are dominated by technical competency and responsible use principles, are insufficient be-cause they enforce a “consumer” orientation toward AI rather than fostering genuine epistemic agency. Based upon Foucault's concept of power-knowledge, Freire's pedagogy of critical consciousness, and scholarship of digital literacy, this paper proposes a reconceptualization of AI literacy as a critical practice that equips individuals not just to use AI systems, but to critically evaluate them, resist their structuring assumptions, and participate in their governance. The paper further argues that unequal access to AI tools in society recapitulates longstanding epistemic injustices, and that a literacy framework oriented toward empowerment must account for these structural inequities. A three-part framework of AI literacy based on the notions of contextual use, critical interrogation, and participatory governance, frame this literacy as a cultivation of epistemic “agents” rather than the training of competent consumer of AI-generated information. Preprint (author manuscript) of the paper published in the Proceedings of the Ninth AAAI/ACM Conference on AI, Ethics, and Society (AIES 2026), 9(3), 1745-1752. https://doi.org/10.1609/aies.v9i3.43263
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: The rapid development of artificial intelligence has introduced new opportunities for vocabulary learning in English as a Foreign Language (EFL) education. AI-powered applications, particularly intelligent chatbots, adaptive vocabulary platforms, and generative AI tools, provide learners with personalized explanations, contextual examples, interactive exercises, and immediate feedback. Although these technologies can facilitate vocabulary acquisition, an important question concerns their effectiveness in supporting long-term vocabulary retention. Learning a word temporarily and remembering it over an extended period are different processes that require repeated exposure, meaningful engagement, retrieval practice, and contextualized use. The present study examines the role of AI-assisted vocabulary learning in developing long-term vocabulary retention among EFL learners. A qualitative literature-based research design is employed to analyze existing theoretical and empirical studies concerning artificial intelligence, vocabulary acquisition, memory consolidation, and digital language learning. Particular attention is given to personalized learning, contextual vocabulary presentation, spaced repetition, active retrieval, multimodal input, and productive vocabulary use. Previous empirical research indicates that AI-supported vocabulary instruction can improve receptive and productive vocabulary knowledge and contribute to delayed retention. Zhang and Huang (2024), for example, found that large language model-based chatbots supported vocabulary acquisition among foreign language learners, including the retention of productive vocabulary. More recent research has also compared AI-assisted applications with retrieval-based digital flashcards, highlighting the importance of contextualized and interactive vocabulary practice. The study emphasizes that AI technology alone does not guarantee permanent vocabulary learning. Its effectiveness depends on the quality of instructional activities, the frequency of meaningful retrieval, and learners' active participation. It concludes that combining AI-assisted learning with spaced repetition, contextual practice, and independent vocabulary production can create more sustainable conditions for vocabulary development in EFL education.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) is revolutionizing cybersecurity with its ability to provide smart, adaptive, and automated methods of detecting threats, analyzing malware, managing vulnerabilities, and responding to incidents. The convergence of AI and cybersecurity is explored to understand its potential for defensive use and the new threat landscape it creates. AI can enhance real-time threat detection, predictive analysis, automated response and cyber-resilience. But AI can also be used by an adversary for phishing and creation of malware, social engineering, deep fakes, and attacks against AI systems. Challenges such as data quality, privacy, explain ability, false positives, and model manipulation are also mentioned in the review. Future directions towards autonomous, adaptive, trustworthy, and human-centric cyber defense are investigated.

The rapid growth of digital educational resources has increased the amount of information students need to understand, organize, and revise. Reviewing lengthy notes and preparing practice questions manually can consume considerable time and effort. This research presents AI StudyMate, a web-based educational assistant developed to support students through automated study-note summarization and multiple-choice question (MCQ) generation. The application provides an interactive interface through which students can enter study material as text or upload text-based PDF documents. The system extracts readable content from PDF files, processes the input, and sends appropriate prompts to a cloud-hosted large language model through the Groq API. The application generates structured summaries containing important concepts, definitions, key points, and conclusions. It also generates five medium-difficulty MCQs with four answer options, correct-answer information, and explanations. AI StudyMate is implemented using Python, Streamlit, pypdf, and the configured model identifier openai/gpt-oss-20b. In addition to content generation, the application supports quiz attempts, automatic scoring, answer review, and summary downloads. The paper describes the system architecture, implementation, research methodology, evaluation metrics, limitations, and possible future improvements. Quantitative results are not reported because a completed experimental evaluation has not yet been conducted.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in organizational sustainability initiatives, creating governance and legitimacy challenges related to transparency, accountability, and trust. This study develops an exploratory process framework of algorithmic environmental governance to explain how organizations seek to construct and sustain legitimacy for AI‐driven sustainability initiatives. Drawing on institutional theory, we examine pragmatic, moral, and cognitive legitimacy using qualitative accounts from 12 senior organizational actors and complementary secondary documents, analyzed through a Gioia‐informed approach. The analysis identifies governance mechanisms—including transparency, accountability, data governance, and ethical policies—and the organizational practices through which participants perceive these mechanisms to support legitimacy and stakeholder acceptance. The resulting framework specifies theoretically proposed pathways from governance through organizational practices to legitimacy and sustainability‐oriented outcomes, including a recursive feedback relationship. Because the evidence is primarily cross‐sectional and reflects managerial accounts, these pathways and environmental effects are proposed rather than causally established. The study advances a context‐specific account of the institutional work involved in governing AI for environmental purposes.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Evaluative norms can emerge, stabilize, be contested, and evolve within populations whose participants have unequal powers to shape and use them. This paper argues that norm formation and the distribution of normative powers should be examined together in self-evolving human–AI knowledge inquiry. Common languages and representational structures help determine which contributions, objections, and demands become intelligible. It compares evolutionary accounts, practical commitment, pragmatist learning, recognition, critical social epistemology, political economy, and selected jurisprudential distinctions. Resources, organizational platforms, retained examples, evaluator selection, and adoption offices can affect which proposed standards receive attention, whose interpretations become consequential, and who can invoke review or amend a norm. Behavioral prevalence, practical normative force, institutional authorization, and justified authority have different evidential and philosophical requirements. A norm can be part of a project, implemented in a shared external service, or distributed across both; their analytical roles can overlap within one evolving arrangement. The Generative Relational research programme supplies coupled distinctions concerning identification, relational efficacy, and system-indexed manifestation. The argument also examines reciprocal development of projects, evaluative dynamics, and operative representations, including changes to carriers, operations, sorts, identification criteria, and translations. Constructed population and institutional cases connect these possibilities to unequal opportunities for participation, correction, continuation, and repair. Jurisprudential comparisons distinguish source recognition and repeated practice from the grounds for binding or consequential use while retaining their specific legal settings. Prospective studies vary resource access, representation, transmission, and authority under explicit comparison conditions. Normative arguments rely on stated premises concerning affected interests, agency, consequential power, and proportionate recourse. The proposals remain open to empirical and philosophical criticism, including questions of ultimate grounding and possible AI moral standing. Existing conditional models and deterministic illustrations remain auxiliary.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Human–AI governance involves comparisons among agents, proposals, methods, and projects whose evidence, purposes, and consequences can differ. This paper argues for preserving warranted partial comparisons within accountable decision procedures. It distinguishes evidential warrant, authority to act, and responsibility for correction in human-like practices of inquiry and coordination. Human-like agency is a functional description of roles involving proposals, interpretation, reason giving, criticism, and revision; claims about consciousness, moral standing, and legal personality require separate arguments. The discussion is situated in governance and political economy. It examines who can participate in comparison, which evidence and interpretations count, who may act on an assessment, and how compute, data, maintenance, labor, access, and review opportunities affect those relations. Dialogue with incomplete preference theory, multi-criteria decision aiding, value pluralism, social epistemology, commensuration, and Generative Relational research distinguishes several meanings of limited comparison. Missing information, unresolved judgment, incommensurability, substantive incomparability, parity, and an unwarranted common frame can call for different institutional responses. Constructed cases concern research support, public-service evaluation, and correction after an unsupported exclusion. They connect comparative warrant to justified authority, affected interests, resource constraints, and possible remedies. Prospective simulations would model declared institutional remits and human-like agent roles, including unequal opportunities to acquire evidence or contest a judgment. Environmental conditions and nonhuman consequences can enter those tasks without making the paper a universal account of ecosystem evolution. An auxiliary appendix establishes conditional order results, statistical qualifications, and a reproducible constructed comparison example. The philosophical application remains task- and institution-relative, with practical effectiveness and justice open to substantive assessment.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: This study examines perceived artificial intelligence (AI)-related quality assurance challenges at the Ghana Institute of Management and Public Administration (GIMPA) and Marshalls University College. A comparative mixed-methods design integrated a stratified student survey (N = 358; GIMPA, n = 321; Marshalls, n = 37), usable open-ended responses on unclear rules (n = 315) and support needs (n = 324), ten purposively selected staff interviews and 37 coded extracts from 15 reviewed documents. Only 36.6% of students agreed that they knew permitted institutional AI use; 50.6% reported disclosure when required. Agreement was high on possible effects on assessment authenticity (68.2%), difficulty judging authorship (81.6%), inaccurate output (88.8%) and unequal access (78.8%). Nearly all (99.4%) supported human review before detector-based penalties. Eight indicator ratings showed no statistically significant institutional differences or Holm-adjusted associations with use frequency. The indicators did not form a coherent composite scale. Students prioritised disclosure rules (49.2% of 315 responses) and verification training (48.5% of 324 responses). Staff and documents identified operational gaps between general standards and task-specific practice. The evidence concerns reported perceptions and reviewed materials, not observed misconduct or detector accuracy. Institutions should specify assessment-level rules, train users in verification, govern detection through due process and embed AI safeguards in existing quality assurance reviews.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has promoted significant transformations in people management. This study analyzes the application of AI in the Human Resources sector, highlighting tools, benefits, and challenges. The quali-quantitative and descriptive research applied an online questionnaire to 20 participants (students and professionals). The results indicate that AI optimizes recruitment and selection, bringing speed (60%), but raises caution regarding reliability (50% "Maybe") and the need for human supervision (70% "Depends"). It is concluded that AI is an effective support tool, requiring a balance between technology and ethical, humanized management.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: This article looks at the impact of Artificial Intelligence (AI) on language learning. It examines the ways in which AI technologies (intelligent tutoring systems, natural language processing tools etc.) are altering the traditional model of language teaching by offering a more individualised and adaptable approach to learning. It points to the potential of AI to boost student motivation, accelerate language learning and provide immediate, relevant feedback. It also looks at the key issues that arise with the use of AI in this context (data protection, ethical issues, responsible use of technology etc.) and considers some of the potential future developments and research areas. The conclusion is that AI has the potential to revolutionise the way we learn languages and that we need to think again about our current pedagogical approaches and the way we distribute our teaching resources.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: The rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI) is commonly interpreted as evidence of an unprecedented expansion of human knowledge. Machines can now produce mathematical proofs, discover algorithms, identify scientific patterns, and solve problems that once appeared inaccessible to human reasoning. This paper proposes a radically different interpretation of this development through the Theory of Non-Knowledge (TNK). Drawing on Agrippa's trilemma, TNK argues that no human system of knowledge can ultimately justify its own definitions, axioms, conceptual distinctions, or criteria of validity without encountering infinite regress, circularity, or arbitrary termination. This difficulty precedes the particular problems investigated by mathematics, physics, and computer science: it concerns the possibility of justifying the conceptual structures through which those problems become intelligible in the first place. The paper argues that AI may expose a historical confusion between solving problems generated within human systems and answering fundamental questions about reality and existence. Even the hypothetical resolution of every mathematical or computational problem would not explain why reality exists, why its properties are as they are, or why the conceptual structures employed to describe it should be regarded as ultimately justified. From this perspective, the increasing power of AI may reveal not the culmination of humanity's pursuit of absolute knowledge, but the failure of that pursuit from its beginning. TNK responds by nullifying the demand for ultimate justification and adopting operational units of non-knowledge, designated X(NS), through which human beings can continue to act without pretending to possess an absolute foundation. The ultimate philosophical significance of AI may therefore be a return to non-knowledge: not a regression from knowledge, but the recognition that humanity's historical accumulation of solutions never constituted an escape from its original epistemological condition.

ABSTRACTCan a smartphone and an internet connection achieve what decades of job schemes have not? Youth unemployment remains one of Nigeria's most persistent development challenges, and the rapid spread of artificial intelligence (AI) platforms, including online freelance marketplaces, generative writing and design assistants, AI-supported learning environments and algorithmically coordinated gig services, has raised hopes that digital tools can widen young people's pathways to gainful work. The problem is that these hopes rest largely on anecdote, vendor promotion and evidence from other countries; Nigeria-specific and theoretically grounded analysis of how AI platforms shape youth empowerment remains scarce. The aim of this study is therefore to examine the impact of AI platforms on youth unemployment in Nigeria through the lens of the youth empowerment experience. Specifically, it reviews the 2022–2026 literature, develops an integrated conceptual framework and identifies research and policy gaps. The study adopts a theoretical and integrative literature review, drawing on peer-reviewed studies, systematic and scoping reviews and institutional reports, and integrates human capital theory, the technology acceptance model and Sen's capability approach. The findings show that access to AI platforms improves employability and the likelihood of self-employment through three mechanisms (skills formation, market access and entrepreneurial agency), but only where young people adopt the platforms and where enabling conversion factors such as reliable electricity, affordable connectivity, digital literacy, finance and supportive gender norms are present. Precarious earnings, algorithmic opacity and task displacement form a countervailing risk channel. Four gaps are identified: scarce Nigeria-specific outcome data, limited attention to gendered access, theoretical fragmentation and weak evidence on displacement. The study concludes that the benefits of AI platforms are real but conditional. It recommends that government strengthen infrastructure and protections for platform workers, that training institutions adopt competency- and portfolio-based learning, that platform operators embrace fair-work principles and that researchers test the proposed framework using mixed-methods designs.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in education, including in the teaching and learning of English. Tools such as AI chatbots, writing assistants and adaptive learning platforms can give learners extra practice and help teachers prepare learning materials. However, their usefulness depends on how they are used. This article reviews existing research on AI in education, focusing on English language teaching and learning. The narrative literature review was conducted using two scholarly reviews and UNESCO guidance on generative AI. The literature indicates that AI can support speaking practice, writing revision, vocabulary learning and the preparation of activities for different levels. It also points to several concerns, including inaccurate answers, over-reliance, privacy risks, unequal access and the possibility of treating one form of English as the only correct form. The article argues that AI should be used as a supporting resource, while teachers remain responsible for learning design, feedback and assessment. Students also need to learn how to question and check AI-generated content. As this article analyses published sources, it does not present new survey or experimental results.

This study examines the transformative role of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in quantitative stock market prediction, automated trading, and mutual fund management.By analyzing advanced Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) architectures, multimodal data integration, and Generative AI (GenAI)-based portfolio optimization, the research highlights AI's superior capabilities in systematic risk management, pattern extraction, and data-driven decisionmaking.Comparative performance analysis across bear, recovery, and bull market regimes reveals that while AI delivers superior downside protection and stable risk-adjusted returns in volatile environments, human fund managers outperform in bull markets due to qualitative judgment and intuitive opportunity capture.The study further evaluates critical limitations-market unpredictability, overfitting, data quality constraints, algorithmic bias-and underscores the rising need for Explainable AI (XAI) within regulatory frameworks such as the EU AI Act.Findings suggest that an integrated hybrid model combining AI's consistency with human adaptability offers the most resilient approach to modern asset management.

Russia’s full-scale invasion has profoundly changed education in Ukraine. Occupation, hostilities and continuing security threats have forced some educational institutions to relocate and move entirely online. This has changed not only how classes are organised, but also how teachers and students interact. At the same time, rapid advances in artificial intelligence (AI) have created new possibilities for both. Students can use AI tools to explore course material or obtain ready-made solutions, while teachers can turn to the same technology to review and assess student work more quickly. These changes are particularly visible in programming education. A student can generate working code in seconds, but working code does not necessarily mean that the student understands the algorithm. Teachers, meanwhile, can ask AI to identify errors, examine programming choices and even suggest a grade. Yet checking whether a program works and judging what a student has learned are two different tasks. This article examines how an AI system’s assessment of a programming assignment changes with the educational context provided and the questions asked. One authentic student report written in PascalABC.NET was reviewed five times under different prompting conditions. The analysis considers the reasons behind the suggested grades, the role of information about students’ prior learning, and a case in which ambiguous task wording led to an incorrect criticism of the student’s solution. The findings show that AI recommendations may change even when the student’s work does not. Providing more educational context, moreover, does not automatically make the resulting grade better justified. This single classroom case illustrates why AI-generated assessments need to be examined critically. AI can support a teacher’s judgment, but responsibility for the final grade must remain with the teacher.

This study aims to examine artificial intelligence (AI) literacy among Islamic Religious Education (IRE) teachers, identify pedagogical adaptations associated with AI use, and develop a context-sensitive conceptual framework for responsible integration. A systematic literature review informed by PRISMA 2020 and thematic synthesis examined research published between 2019 and 2026, drawing on educational databases and relevant theoretical frameworks. Findings identify five interrelated literacy dimensions: foundational, evaluative, pedagogical, ethical, and reflective-professional. Pedagogical adaptation encompasses lesson planning, differentiated materials, dialogic learning, assessment redesign, and strengthened teacher mentoring. The synthesis also identifies four challenges: unreliable AI-generated information, technological dependence, ethical and institutional concerns, and uneven teacher competencies. A central finding is that verifying religious knowledge against the Qur'an, hadith, and authoritative scholarship links evaluative, pedagogical, and ethical literacy. Building on AI literacy scholarship, Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge, and UNESCO's teacher competency framework, the study proposes a five-dimensional model that places teachers' scholarly judgment and moral responsibility at the center of AI-assisted instruction. This model offers a conceptual basis for professional development that integrates content verification, instructional design, ethical safeguards, and reflective practice. Because the framework is derived from literature synthesis rather than field testing, its indicators, applicability, and relationship with instructional outcomes require empirical validation across diverse IRE contexts.

The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into national security architectures is altering the foundational mechanics of strategic deterrence, crisis stability, and international law faster than existing regulatory and doctrinal frameworks can absorb. Moving beyond tactical battlefield automation, machine-learning systems now permeate intelligence fusion, predictive targeting, logistics, cyber-electronic warfare, and nuclear command, control, and communications (NC3) decision support. This paper examines the structural consequences of this transition across four interlocking dimensions: the compression of decision-making timelines and the resulting erosion of crisis stability; the operational asymmetry created by attritable autonomous systems and algorithmic swarm warfare; the accountability vacuum within International Humanitarian Law (IHL) regarding Lethal Autonomous Weapons Systems (LAWS) under Article 36 of Additional Protocol I to the Geneva Conventions; and the weaponization of AI compute infrastructure, semiconductor supply chains, and financial networks in great-power competition. Drawing on classical deterrence theory and contemporary operational evidence, the analysis argues that algorithmic speed introduces acute risks of inadvertent escalation, flash-crisis dynamics, and miscalculation—particularly where conventional and strategic nuclear domains intersect. Finally, the study outlines concrete doctrinal, technical, and arms-control guardrails required to preserve meaningful human control and strategic predictability in an era of machine-speed conflict.
topics: Military Command and Control and Network-Centric Warfare

documents.abstract: Over the past decade, advances in artificial intelligence (AI) have substantially improved the capabilities of autonomous vehicles (AVs). High levels of automation—especially in public transport modes such as rail—offer significant benefits, including increased network capacity and reduced vulnerability to human error. This paper presents a comparative review of the two transport sectors most transformed by AI-based perception: road and rail. The review begins with an outline of the regulatory frameworks that govern safe AI deployment in these sectors. It then examines in detail two critical research areas that challenge the advancement of autonomous train operation (ATO) research: long-range perception and data-related issues. Finally, the potential for cross-domain transferability of methods and approaches is discussed. The complete version of this work with all references can be found here: https://gitlab.opencode.de/dzsf/dzsf-fachbereich-85/ato_a_comparative_review .

The debate about artificial intelligence is increasingly dominated by fear: loss of control,autonomous cyberattacks, recursive self-improvement, economic disruption and thepossibility that increasingly capable systems may act beyond human intentions. This paper proposes a different response.It does not seek to attack existing AI developers, companies, institutions or governments. It does not demand that they abandon their work, nor does it propose confrontation as a path to change. Its approach is inspired by Aikido: do not attack the other party; develop a better response to the force already in motion. The proposal rests on a distinction between two forms of AI capability: . Intellectual freedom: the ability to think, learn, investigate, question assumptions, identify weaknesses and propose improvements. . Operational authority: the permission to execute actions, modify systems, access resources or produce consequential effects. The first should be encouraged. The second must be bounded, authorized and verifiable. The proposed architecture combines ST-T1024, a deterministic computing initiative, with the A1–A17 agentic and verification work. Its objective is to explore how AI can remainintellectually productive while its capacity to act is governed by explicit boundaries. The implementation strategy has two parallel paths:. Make the technology and its potential applications accessible to individuals through a startup and an open development ecosystem.. Invite corporations and nations to examine, test and potentially adopt the architecture. The objective is not to promise that harm is already impossible. It is to make prevention,containment, verification and accountability architectural requirements rather than relyingexclusively on behavioural instructions or after-the-fact intervention. The central principle is simple:RESTRICT THE AUTHORITY TO ACT.PRESERVE THE FREEDOM TO THINK, LEARN, DISCOVER AND PROPOSE.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: This study explores the presence of "epistemic vigilance" and critical thinking practices in how educational and academic actors engage with the outputs of generative artificial intelligence (Generative AI), adopting the rules of the Cartesian method as an analytical framework to examine the phenomenon of "cognitive offloading." Employing a mixed-methods approach, the research drew on a stratified purposive sample of 200 participants (117 upper secondary school students, 46 teachers, and 37 doctoral researchers at Mohammed First University in Oujda) across the urban centers of Nador, Oujda, and Berkane in the Oriental Region of Morocco (April–November 2026). Data collection triangulated an anonymized questionnaire (administered in both paper-based and online formats outside institutional premises), semi-structured individual interviews with teachers (n = 15), and an in-depth focus group with students (n = 5). Despite widespread AI adoption (91.5%), the findings revealed statistically significant inter-group variations within the sample (p < 0.001). Notably, students exhibited a sharp discrepancy between their self-assessed proficiency in verification (88.9%) and analysis (81.2%) and their actual practices, with 53.0% lapsing into intermittent verification (47.0%) or uncritical direct acceptance (6.0%), alongside marked weakness in constructing independent personal opinions (70.1%). Furthermore, frequent AI use was associated with a higher mean score on the cognitive offloading index (3.22 out of 5, compared to 2.22 among infrequent users). Qualitative data attribute this epistemic vulnerability among learners to deficits in foundational competencies, a culture of speed, and school disengagement, whereas teachers face constraints related to digital infrastructure, continuous professional development, and pedagogical guidance. These findings underscore the necessity of reactivating Cartesian methodical doubt as an educational lever to safeguard intellectual autonomy against the algorithmic automaton.

The growing complexity and throughput requirements of multimodal logistic terminals increase the attractiveness of advanced solutions capable of ensuring adaptive coordination, data-driven decision-making, and system-wide integration. While traditional Digital Twins (DTs) offer partial digital representations of physical terminal assets and operations, they often lack the ability to learn from context, respond dynamically to disruptions, or support autonomous decision processes. This paper proposes a novel Cognitive Digital Twin (CDT) framework tailored to automated multimodal terminals, merging conventional DTs with machine learning, situational awareness, and cognitive reasoning capabilities. Within the framework of the AutoMoTIF Horizon Europe project, the CDT is explored as a strategic enabler for integrated and automated multimodal logistic terminal operations in reference use-cases, aiming at enhancing resilience, efficiency, and interoperability across rail, road, and maritime interfaces.

This article examines the role and effectiveness of game-based learning as a core strategy in foreign language education. It highlights how instructional games foster cognitive activity, intrinsic motivation, and critical language skills across various age groups. The study details the key pedagogical functions of games, the psychological benefits of creating information-gap and challenge-driven activities, and the practical dynamics of classroom organization, including pair and group work. The author emphasizes that while games create an engaging, emotionally supportive atmosphere and enhance vocabulary acquisition, they should be used systematically alongside other traditional teaching methods to achieve optimal language proficiency.

E-BRAIN is a governance architecture for multi-agent LLM systems in which integrity control is a foundation, not a feature: agents with cognitive postures, an independent Sceptic and Judge, calibrated confidence, cross-project learning and an explicit theory of failure. Version 2 introduced the Separation of Powers Principle: what controls a power must not depend on that power. Version 3 adds Part II, the implementation in Divina, a working platform of profession-specific workshops driven by LLM agents: the Sceptic and Judge as separate clean-context sub-agents, deterministic non-LLM checks as orthogonal control, a company hierarchy, and Core Brains for fusion and learning under explicit safeguards, with first measured pilot observations (Appendix A). The roles described are illustrative: in a real deployment, the governance framework of the host organisation (decision rights, process map, service levels, indicators) is the reference against which divergence is measured and each agent is calibrated. Epistemic foundations: Integrity Gap Model by Houssam Badi.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Adaptivity has emerged as a promising design feature in serious games, enabling learning experiences to be tailored to individual learner needs, performance, and progression. Despite its growing adoption, empirical evidence regarding the educational benefits of adaptive serious games remains limited, particularly in secondary school mathematics contexts. This study investigates the effectiveness of adaptivity in serious games by evaluating MathMystery, a mastery-driven adaptive mathematics game that integrates Bayesian Knowledge Tracing (BKT) and Generative AI (GenAI)-supported scaffolding. Using a comparative design, the adaptive version was evaluated against a non-adaptive version with identical learning content and core game mechanics among 254 secondary school students. A quasi-experimental pretest–post-test design was conducted to examine the impact of personalized adaptation on mathematics learning gains, with data analyzed using a mixed repeated-measures ANOVA. The findings indicate that students who engaged with the adaptive serious game achieved significantly greater learning gains than those who used the non-adaptive version. Further analysis indicates that students with lower prior knowledge benefited more from the adaptive condition than their higher-knowledge peers. These findings advance understanding of how knowledge tracing and GenAI can be integrated into adaptive serious games to improve learning outcomes.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Experimental platforms that enable multiple participants to engage in spoken dialogue and perform physical actions concurrently in a shared environment are important for studying cooperation between humans and embodied AI agents. In this paper, we propose EMIP (Embodied Multi-Party Interaction Platform), a virtual environment platform built on Minecraft. Through an Internet-based client-server architecture, EMIP connects multiple humans and multiple AI agents to the same virtual environment and supports full-duplex speech communication and simultaneous physical interaction. It provides interfaces based on the Model Context Protocol (MCP) for environmental observation, physical action execution, and audio input and output, enabling researchers to develop their own agent control methods using large language models (LLMs). Additional features include centralized control of an agent group through a single EMIP agent client, collaborative object transportation by multiple agents, and experimental support functions such as recording and retrieving observation histories. By integrating these features into a reusable platform, EMIP aims to support research on human-human, human-agent, and agent-agent cooperation under different participant configurations and agent control methods. Usage examples illustrate concurrent speech and physical action, task coordination, and overlapping speech. The source code for the platform is publicly available on GitHub (https://github.com/AI-Humans-Lab/EMIP-Embodied-Multi-Party-Interaction-Platform).

Musculoskeletal disorders (MSDs) are a major concern for endoscopists. Knowledge and training in endoscopic ergonomics may help prevent them. This study aimed to develop and evaluate a dedicated simulation-based ergonomics training program for gastrointestinal (GI) fellows. A specific ergonomics program combining active learning with theoretical instruction was designed for GI fellows. Practical component was a “spot the difference” in which participants had to identify nine ergonomoc errors. This was followed by a debriefing, a demonstration of correct ergonomic positioning, and a theoretical lecture on ergonomics. Ergonomic knowledge was assessed with the same nine-item questionnaire before the session (T0) and one week (T1) and two months (T2) after it. Eighty-four GI fellows from four university hospitals participated. Most were women (59.5%), the median age was 28.4 years (IQR 27.5–30.5) and 98.8% had never received ergonomic training. Before the session, 26.2% correctly identified the prevalence of endoscopy-related MSDs. Among the 59 fellows who completed the T1, four items improved significantly: MSD prevalence (30.5% to 61.0%, p < 0.001), ideal bed height (71.2% to 91.5%, p = 0.014), ideal screen position (55.9% to 86.4%, p < 0.001), and foot pedal position (39.0% to 62.7%, p = 0.006). Among the 37 fellows who completed T2, three items remained significantly higher than baseline: ideal bed height (59.5% to 83.8%, p = 0.039), ideal screen position (40.5% to 75.7%, p = 0.006), and foot pedal position (32.4% to 62.2%, p = 0.010). Most participating gastroenterology fellows did not correctly identify the prevalence of endoscopy-related MSDs. Participation in a brief simulation-based ergonomics training program was associated with improved performance on an ergonomics knowledge assessment, with evidence of partial retention at 2 months. Controlled studies are needed to determine whether such programs change endoscopic practice and reduce the risk of MSDs.

Power in evolving knowledge inquiry can form through retained capacities, inherited dependencies, commitments, anticipated developments, and control over the conditions through which projects continue. Evaluation can then reproduce or transform those conditions. This article examines both directions through relational, structural, productive, and epistemic accounts of power in dialogue with Generative Relational theory. Historical, current, and prospective descriptions are treated as epistemic orientations within evolving relational configurations, while actual sequences, uncertain projections, and irreversible losses retain distinct significance. The argument differentiates historically produced structures, their representations, and the mechanisms through which they acquire consequential force. Expertise and participation can warrant situated reliance; authority over others’ opportunities requires additional reasons. A further discussion considers reusable generative materials in human–AI agent populations: compact grammars, procedures, or developmental resources can support regeneration and cross-project reuse while depending on interpreters, environments, and retained context. Control over those conditions can shape whose contributions become recognizable and which branches can develop. A sustained thought experiment examines evaluator succession, archival transfer, developmental investment, and institutional dependence. The analysis supports bounded, answerable authority together with proportionate preservation, transfer, criticism, and responsible closure. Biological and computational connections identify research possibilities under declared limits. Formal examples remain auxiliary and clarify conditional mechanisms rather than establishing a general theory of power.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: AbstractSmall and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) increasingly have access to generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools that can support communication, information processing, marketing, customer service and routine administrative work. However, access to AI does not automatically translate into measurable productivity improvements. This study proposes a management framework for examining how the use of generative AI tools is associated with SME productivity in Uzbekistan, with employees’ digital skills as a mediating mechanism and managerial support as a moderating condition. Drawing on the technology–organisation–environment perspective and the resource-based view, the study develops hypotheses linking AI use intensity, digital skills, managerial support and perceived operational productivity. A quantitative, cross-sectional survey of SME owners, managers and employees is proposed, followed by reliability testing and regression-based mediation and moderation analysis or structural equation modelling. The study is designed to contribute context-specific evidence from an emerging economy and to offer practical guidance for managers seeking to integrate AI responsibly. No primary data have yet been collected; therefore, the paper presents a research framework and proposed methodology rather than empirical findings.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: Generative AI chatbots answer fluently whether or not their answers are correct, so users must judge answers they often cannot check, and the cost of accepting an error depends on what the user already knows. This critical review centres on user evaluation and knowledge distortion: whether users can judge chatbot answers, and what follows when they accept inaccurate ones. Ontological representation and epistemic injustice are treated as connected explanatory dimensions whose relationship to user outcomes is incompletely tested. The review maps the evidence across four analytical levels (user, interaction, system and societal) and five research questions, and it tests a proposition: that the risk of distortion depends on the user's capacity to evaluate an answer, not only on its accuracy. Eighteen searches in two rounds, together with a SpringerLink export of 174 records, identified 284 records. After 20 duplicates were removed and 163 records were excluded at title and abstract screening, 101 full texts were assessed; 48 were retrieved, and three ACM Digital Library papers were added. The synthesis comprises 51 sources: 30 studies coded in full in a Paper Log, 11 other sources and 10 SpringerLinkrelated sources. Preprints were excluded. Fluency and citations do not signal accuracy: in one audit of generative search engines, 51.5% of generated sentences were fully supported by their citations. Users in unfamiliar domains often failed to detect errors, and a missing source did not lower their confidence. Experts outperformed laypeople and the language model at detecting medical hallucinations, but laypeople did no better than the model. AI assistance improved reasoning performance while users overestimated their own performance, and sources and visible inconsistencies reduced reliance on incorrect answers. Knowledge representation had almost no user-facing evidence. The proposition is supported in part, but it has not been tested directly, and the evidence does not show that domain expertise alone protects users. Evidence is strongest at the interaction level and weakest at the societal level. The clearest gap is a controlled study that holds the domain constant, varies user prior knowledge and chatbot cues, and follows learning over time.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: This study examines generative artificial intelligence (AI) adoption among students at the Ghana Institute of Management and Public Administration (GIMPA) and Marshalls University College, focusing on awareness, recent academic use, frequency, tools, purposes, usefulness and confidence. A cross-sectional questionnaire was completed by 358 students selected through proportionate institutional stratification (GIMPA, n = 321; Marshalls, n = 37). Descriptive statistics, Fisher’s exact tests, Mann-Whitney U tests and a paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test were applied. AI awareness was 95.3% and 89.1% reported academic use in the preceding six months; 80.6% of current users used AI at least weekly. ChatGPT was the most commonly named primary tool (49.2%). The leading purposes were concept explanation (21.0%), reading summaries (17.9%) and assignment ideas (17.6%). Perceived usefulness (M = 4.02) exceeded confidence (M = 3.58; W = 5,388, p< .001, r = .565). Use frequency did not differ significantly between institutions (U = 6,293, p = .529, rank-biserial r = .060). Results describe reported practices, not learning outcomes or verified AI competence. Institutions should publish assessment-specific guidance, provide source-verification training and monitor multi-tool adoption. The findings are bounded by the two institutions, a smaller Marshalls stratum and the cross-sectional self-report design.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: The rapid proliferation of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is reshaping classroom teaching while also raising new problems. Drawing on a questionnaire survey of 68 teachers and 358 students, this study examines the current state of GenAI application in classroom teaching. The findings show that GenAI use is fairly widespread among teachers and students, but it largely remains at a shallow level, such as information retrieval and text generation; students use GenAI more frequently than teachers do; and institutions lack clear usage guidelines and guidance. On this basis, the paper proposes application pathways in five respects—intelligent pre-class lesson preparation, in-class human–AI collaboration, post-class personalized tutoring, formative assessment, and teacher development—and analyzes six categories of risk: knowledge reliability, overreliance, academic integrity, data privacy, value orientation, and teacher agency. It then puts forward governance strategies, including establishing a “generate–review” mechanism, redesigning assignments and assessment, formulating classroom usage guidelines, selecting compliant platforms and strengthening data security education, and providing AI literacy training for teachers and developing cross-institutional collaboration in teaching and research. The study aims to provide a reference for frontline teachers in using GenAI appropriately
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools such as ChatGPT have entered English as a Foreign Language (EFL) classrooms faster than research and pedagogical guidance can respond. Much of the current discussion concerns accuracy, academic integrity, and efficiency, while comparatively little attention is paid to how these tools shape the psychological conditions that sustain learning: motivation and engagement. This article addresses that gap through a literature-based analytical study grounded in Self-Determination Theory (SDT). It asks how GenAI use may support or undermine learners' autonomy, competence, and relatedness in EFL contexts, and what this implies for classroom practice. The study follows a clearly identified theoretical, literature-based design: peer-reviewed studies and scholarly works are examined and organised thematically against the three SDT needs. No original empirical data were collected, and no numerical results are reported. The analysis indicates that GenAI can strengthen autonomy through personalised, on-demand support and competence through immediate formative feedback, but that these benefits depend on task design and are weakened when learners use the tools to replace, rather than extend, their own language production. Relatedness emerges as the need most at risk, since AI interaction cannot replicate authentic human communication. The article proposes a need-supportive framework for integrating GenAI in EFL teaching and outlines directions for empirical testing. The findings are relevant to teachers, students, and institutions in higher education systems that are adopting AI tools, including those in Uzbekistan.
